title: Technical trading in the Santa Fe Institute Artificial Stock Market revisited
publisher: Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization (Elsevier), vol. 61(4), pp. 599-616; author Norman Ehrentreich

key_points.claim: Re-examines evidence of technical trading in the Santa Fe Artificial Stock Market, given an upwardly biased mutation operator in the original model.
key_points.evidence_quote: reconsiders evidence of technical trading in the Santa Fe Artificial Stock Market in light of an upwardly biased mutation operator

key_points.claim: An alternative mutation operator shows no technical trading, but two other tests still establish that technical trading exists.
key_points.evidence_quote: While an alternative mutation operator points to no technical trading, two tests other than the inappropriate investigation of the aggregate bit level establish the existence of technical trading beyond a doubt.

key_points.claim: Genetic drift is an important evolutionary force in the agents' learning. The paper gives tools for judging the relative importance of selection and drift.
key_points.evidence_quote: identifies genetic drift as an important evolutionary force and provides tools to judge the relative importance of selection and genetic drift with arbitrary mutation operators

key_points.claim: When selection is weak, persistent technical trading is consistent with the Efficient Market Hypothesis.
key_points.evidence_quote: when selective forces are weak, the continued existence of technical trading can be reconciled with the Efficient Market Hypothesis

reliability_notes: Abstract only (ScienceDirect page, full text not retrieved). Peer-reviewed journal article. Relevant to the learning and evolution of agents and to market institutions in artificial stock markets.
